Noble Audio's Astrid have a triple-driver system and sleek looks .

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Noble Audio has had one seriously busy year in 2026, and it's not over yet. The Texas-based company has impressed us with in-ear monitors and over-ear cans alike, from the Lu Ban wired IEMs made from cocobolo wood to the Noble FoKus Artemis over-ear ANC headphones, which we gave a near-perfect 4.5-star review.

Now, it's adding another wireless in-ear headphone to its lineup. The Astrid will sit somewhere in the middle of its current offering, so they won't enter our pick of the best budget IEMs, but they offer an intriguing proposition: three driver technologies for the ability to both adapt sound to your own unique hearing profile and adjust it to how you want it to sound.

They look sharp too with an intricate silver-toned frost-like pattern over the glass fiber earbud and the charging case.

Hybrid earphones are a familiar territory for Noble Audio, which has explored driver combinations in its universal and custom in-ear monitors. Astrid brings that experience to a new wireless design.

There are three driver technologies in each ear piece: an 8.3mm dynamic driver, 6mm planar driver and a balanced armature. The first uses a PU diaphragm with an aluminium-magnesium alloy dome. This works alongside the other two technologies in a hybrid system that takes account of differences between your left and right ears as well as the way your hearing differs from other people’s.

Using Audiodo Personal Sound, a short test checks each ear and creates a personal hearing profile. This is then used to adjust playback to your ears. Meanwhile, the Audiodo Equalizer allows you to adjust bass, mids and treble as preferred: the result is sound that accounts for both how you hear and how you like your music to sound, the company says.

The new TWS has Active Noise Cancellation and a Transparency mode to let through outside sound when needed. Microphone noise and wind reduction are intended to help with calls, while Bluetooth 6.0 and two-device multipoint make it possible to keep a phone and laptop connected at the same time.

Noble cites up to 11 hours of listening per charge and up to 40 hours including the case, depending on settings, with USB-C and wireless charging. There's a choice of silicone ear tips, and the buds have IPX4 splash resistance.

Priced at $539 / £499, the Astrid sits above the $200 Osprey and the Rex5 but below the flagship Prestige Encore II in Noble's growing TWS range. You can order at nobleaudio.com and selected retailers.

I Visited China as an American Without a Visa—Here’s How You Can Do It Too

📅 Nov 10, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Last month, I visited China as an American—without going through a multi-week visa application process. This is thanks to a recent policy introduced in 2024 that allows certain travelers to visit China for a maximum of 10 days while transiting between one country and another. Though the rule can feel intimidating in theory, it’s relatively straightforward in practice as long as you prepare accordingly.

Officially called the “240-Hour Visa-Free Transit Policy," the program is part of China’s goal to attract more inbound international travelers, according to Mei Zhang, the founder of WildChina and a Condé Nast Traveler travel specialist. “The idea is to make visiting China an easier decision,” Zhang says. “Most people are daunted by the idea of queuing for a visa at the Chinese consulate. Removing that step makes it easier for people to come.”

And even though the policy is designed for transiting between countries, 10 days is still enough time for a meaningful visit. “Beyond the quick business visits or short stopovers people may associate with China, ten days gives travelers time to explore several destinations, experience the culture, and develop a deeper appreciation for the country,” says Catherine Heald, CNT specialist and founder of Remote Lands, which specializes in travel to Asia.

However, because the program is relatively new, not all airline or airport staff are familiar with it—which almost resulted in me being denied boarding. To help you avoid ending up in a similar situation, here’s what travelers should know before booking your flight to China, so you too can see the Forbidden City in Beijing, the futuristic skyline glowing along the Bund in Shanghai, the terracotta warriors in Xi'an, and the mountainous megacity of Chongqing.

Officially called the “240-Hour Visa-Free Transit Policy,” this new rule was first introduced by China’s National Immigration Administration in December 2024. It permits a traveler to visit China without obtaining a visa ahead of time as long as the total length of their stay in the country does not exceed 240 hours. “It’s a great policy that has driven the growth of international travelers to China,” says Zhang, “but you do need to read the fine print before using it.”

The fine print: First of all, the operative word is transit. You have to enter China from one country, then leave it for another, different country. For example, flying from the US to China, then from China to Japan is allowed. However, going from the US to China, then back to the US, is not. Hong Kong, Macao, and Taiwan count as separate destinations for this policy, so a trip that goes from Hong Kong to mainland China to Taiwan would qualify for a visa-free transit in China that does not last longer than 10 days.

Second: Only holders of passports from 57 countries, including the United States, can take advantage of this policy. See the full list here. And third: You have to enter and exit via designated ports. The full list is here, and it conveniently includes the cities you might visit on a first-time visit to China, like Beijing, Shanghai, and Chengdu. If you want to travel beyond the areas permitted by the transit policy, you’ll have to apply for a Chinese visa.

“Remember that you can enter and leave through the same eligible Chinese city or choose different eligible cities,” says Heald of Remote Lands. So you could come to China through Shanghai, spend three days there, then take the high-speed train to Beijing, stay for another three days, then depart for a third destination like nearby South Korea to make the most out of your trip.

The Forbidden City was the Chinese imperial palace from the Ming dynasty to the end of the Qing dynasty (1420-1912).

To try the transit policy for myself, I kept my first-ever trip to China simple. I arrived in Shanghai on September 30 and departed on October 5, entering and exiting through the same qualifying port, Shanghai Pudong International Airport (PVG). I stayed in the country for a total of five nights, well under the 240-hour limit. (For what it’s worth, I stayed at the good-looking PuLi Shanghai, the very cool Upper House Shanghai, and the historically rich Capella Shanghai, Jian Ye Li, to explore different parts of the city.)

I’m an American citizen, so my US passport made me eligible for the transit policy. As for my routing, I departed from Paris, where I live, on a direct flight to Shanghai; from there I flew onward to Manila. The logic is that this made my visit to China count as a long layover since my final destination was actually the Philippines.

As you prepare your itinerary, check—and double check—that your passport, routing, entry and departure ports in China, and destinations within China all qualify under the 240-hour visa-free transit policy before you make your bookings. The list of qualifying passports and entry-exit ports in China can be found here.

Once you have all your confirmation info, it’s a good idea to get organized and put together a folder with all your bookings as proof of your plans to stay no more than 10 days in China. “Carry printed copies of your confirmed onward tickets, hotel reservations, and itinerary,” Heald says. She also recommends calling your airline before departure and confirming your transit eligibility with them. You might even print the official page describing the policy (again, here!) so you can present it to anyone you encounter, like a check-in agent, who might be unfamiliar with the relatively new 10-day rule.

Consider this your heads up, says Zhang: “It’s a great policy but sometimes the implementation on the ground can be uneven.” For an added layer of security, consider booking your travel to China with local tour operators or travel specialists like WildChina or Remote Lands. They can design a trip that will definitely qualify for the transit policy, and can help you out in case you run into issues while you’re traveling.

Well, I did none of the above. I arrived at Paris-Charles de Gaulle for my flight to Shanghai without any printed confirmations of my onward ticket to Manila, my three hotel stays, or the official policy from the Chinese National Immigration Administration’s official website.

The Air France check-in agent asked me to present my Chinese visa, which, of course, I did not have. I tried to explain in French that I could go to China through this new policy, but the agent insisted, “Non, c’est pas possible.” Foolishly, I plugged “10-day visa-free transit China” into Google on my phone and presented the results to him. He sighed, switched to English, and said, “That is not official. That is AI Overview.”

I asked if there was anyone at Air France I could talk to, and the agent shook his head. Maybe he softened when he saw the panic creep across my face because he then phoned a colleague, an Air France agent who was Chinese. The other agent explained that I was correct, there is indeed a new 10-day transit policy, and all I had to do was present my onward ticket to the Philippines, which I did have saved as a screenshot on my phone.

May my failure to properly prepare be your reminder to print out everything, including your flight and accommodation info, as well as the official visa-free transit policy. If there was ever a time to be a type-A traveler, it’s this.

Once in China, the process becomes much smoother. All international travelers are required to fill out a digital arrival form, whether they have a visa or not. The form asks if you have a visa for China and, when you select no, offers a drop-down menu where you can declare that you are visiting through the 240-hour visa-free transit policy. Once that’s done, the form gives you a QR code that confirms you’ve completed the form; screenshot this code, just in case. Then go through the immigration line, approach the immigration officer, and present whatever is asked of you, like that QR code or your onward ticket, when prompted. That’s it!

For my journey, I got to Pudong Airport in Shanghai, logged onto the airport Wi-Fi, completed the form, and went into the immigration line. They didn’t ask for the QR code but they did ask for my ticket to Manila. Once everything looked good to them, they stamped my passport with a transit visa—a little sticker that declared my date of entry into China and when they expected me to leave. I was cleared to go, and I stepped into the duty-free shopping area, located right before baggage claim, feeling giddy and satisfied that it all worked out.

Zhang says working with a travel company could help relieve some of the stress on the arrival side too: “WildChina normally would book a VIP airport pickup if any of our travelers are using the 10-day transit visa. This way, an airport concierge would meet the guests at the gate and walk them through the visa step-by-step. This eases the stress of facing an unfamiliar bureaucratic process.”

One of the things that greatly intimidated me about visiting China was how different the tech is. There’s no Uber or Google Maps, which has been very helpful for me on my solo travels in new-to-me countries. The very fine teams at PuLi Shanghai and Upper House Shanghai helped me get set up with the right apps, and I was zipping around the city in no time. (For a map app, Apple Maps worked like a charm, to my surprise.) Here are tips for what Chinese apps to download before traveling.

First, set up Alipay, which is a do-it-all app and a total lifeline in China. You can link an international bank card and use it for all payments everywhere you go; call a DiDi car (China’s equivalent of Uber or Lyft), use its translation tool, and more. “Alipay is part of everyday life here,” Zhang says. “At most restaurants, you can scan the QR code on your table with Alipay, choose your dishes—already translated on the interface—and pay through the app.” Be sure to set it up and link your bank account or card before you arrive in China; some verification steps require authorization via your phone number, which you may not have access to while in the country.

Second, everyone in China is on WeChat, so you’d do well to download that too; it’s how I communicated with the guest experiences team at Capella Shanghai, Jian Ye Li, who took me on cultural tours in the hotel’s neighborhood. Think of it as Chinese WhatsApp.

And to stay connected online, Heald suggests checking if your existing carrier offers roaming in mainland China (helpful for any verification texts you may need to receive). Otherwise, get a compatible travel eSIM that explicitly covers it. A home carrier or a travel eSIM will allow you to connect to sites like Google Workplace and apps like Instagram that you would not be able to normally access through the internet while in China. For my phone, Airalo, a travel eSIM, and Free, my French home carrier, worked perfectly.

“If you'll be using a laptop or tablet on Wi-Fi and need access to services such as Google, WhatsApp, or Instagram, install a VPN and arrange any paid subscription before you leave,” Zhang says. “Downloading and setting it up can be much trickier once you're in China.” I, for one, used Astrill VPN to stay connected on my laptop to sites like Gmail and YouTube.

And finally, both Zhang and Heald recommend keeping an open mind. “China can feel very different from what you know,” Heald says. “Give yourself the chance to observe, ask questions and learn, rather than expecting everything to feel familiar.” Zhang adds, “That's part of getting to know a place. Don’t be afraid to ask for help or start a conversation, even if you only have a few words in common. You'll often find people are curious about you too, and pleased that you've come to see where they live.”

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

Mini Review: Warhammer Survivors (PS5) - Absurdly Addictive Crossover Is a Match Made in Bullet Hell

📅 Nov 10, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Warhammer Survivors is exactly what its name suggests: a Warhammer reskin of Vampire Survivors.

Developed by licensed Warhammer studio Auroch Digital, with Vampire Survivors creator poncle partnering on the project, it's a fantastic, heartfelt adaptation right out of the gate.

Indeed, it's immediately obvious that an awful lot of care has been taken in providing poncle's world-beating gameplay formula with a fresh coat of paint. The Warhammer settings, characters, enemies, and weapons are all there — but the game also relishes in dishing out smaller references to Games Workshop's immensely popular fiction.

In particular, I was left pleasantly surprised by how often Warhammer Survivors pays tribute to the property's tabletop identity. Numerous playable characters, for example, are unlocked by finding miniature figure paints scattered across maps.

Meanwhile, power ups can include rolling damage dice — actual dice — across the battlefield, crushing your foes in the process. You can even drop giant blast radius templates on top of your enemies if you're lucky.

What I'm saying is that Auroch Digital and poncle clearly had loads of fun with this one — it's not just a simple copy and paste job that takes advantage of the Warhammer name.

Oh, and it's basically two games in one. On the main menu, you can pick between Warhammer's dark sci-fi 40,000 setting, and its high fantasy Age of Sigmar setting. Each comes with its own character roster, maps, enemy factions, objectives, upgrades, and everything else, making for a seriously robust package.

Gameplay-wise, the title offers a slight twist on the absurdly addictive Survivors structure. Stages have a 25-minute time limit instead of 30, and I'd say there's a larger emphasis on tactical thinking.

That's because specialised opponents are more prevalent, forcing you to weave your way through the hordes in a more methodical manner. At least, until you rack up so many super-powered upgrades that anything in your path just evaporates anyway.

Yep, that same progression curve that makes Vampire Survivors so insanely moreish is alive and well here, although I do think it takes a little longer to hit those truly chaotic highs because of the aforementioned tweaks.

All in all, Warhammer Survivors perfectly melds Games Workshop's property with poncle's timeless formula, resulting in another exceptional roguelike experience.

TL;DR: American Bitcoin reported approximately $126 million in third-quarter net income and said its Bitcoin reserve increased through mining rather than new spot purchases during the period. The November 4 release also cites about $221 million in adjusted EBITDA and an approximately 5% increase in satoshis per share.

American Bitcoin reported approximately $126 million in third-quarter net income and said its Bitcoin reserve increased through mining rather than new spot purchases during the period. The November 4 release also cites about $221 million in adjusted EBITDA and an approximately 5% increase in satoshis per share. Those figures put the focus on an increasingly important distinction among public Bitcoin businesses: the difference between growing a treasury and growing the amount of Bitcoin attributable to each share.

The company says it did not issue shares through its at-the-market program or purchase Bitcoin during the quarter. Instead, management credits mining operations with reserve growth despite seasonal electricity cost pressure. It also highlights a roughly 5% increase in sats per share. This metric is worth checking because a rising total Bitcoin balance can be less impressive if the share count rises even faster. Yet sats per share is not an accounting profit measure or a guarantee of shareholder return. Investors also need to consider debt, other assets and liabilities, operating expenses and the market price paid for the stock.

American Bitcoin reported net income and adjusted EBITDA of different magnitudes. Adjusted EBITDA can help explain management's view of operating performance, but exclusions and accounting policies matter. In mining and treasury companies, the price of Bitcoin, the valuation of held assets, depreciation of mining equipment and financing arrangements can all materially affect results. A single strong quarter should therefore be read beside the company's complete financial statements and reconciliation of non-GAAP figures. Comparing adjusted EBITDA from two miners is difficult unless the underlying definitions are aligned.

Management describes producing Bitcoin at a structural discount to market prices. Miners can achieve attractive unit costs when power contracts, fleet efficiency and site economics are favorable, but network difficulty and Bitcoin's price constantly change the equation. Electricity costs can be seasonal; new mining capacity can increase competition; older machines can become less efficient. A production model that looks profitable today may be less attractive after a difficult market shift. It is useful to track the cost of mining one coin, but readers should ask exactly which direct and indirect costs are included.

Public shareholders own claims on a company, not specific coins in its reserve. That provides exposure to mining operations and management decisions as well as the Bitcoin held. The company can create value through efficient production and disciplined capital allocation, but it can also face stock-market volatility unrelated to the daily Bitcoin move. The most meaningful comparison with direct BTC ownership is not merely whether its reserves rise, but whether shareholders benefit after dilution, corporate costs and valuation premiums are considered.

The next quarter should be assessed using mined BTC, treasury changes, production cost, network difficulty, share count and cash liquidity. The company's earnings release is a useful snapshot, but it does not make future mining profitability predictable. In a sector where several operators are selling Bitcoin to fund AI data centers, American Bitcoin's stated emphasis on accumulating coins provides a distinct business model for investors to evaluate.

Anthropic enters student AI privacy agreement with teachers unions

📅 Nov 10, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Let K-12 Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

AFT President Randi Weingarten said she hopes the safeguards for the tech will one day be “embedded in law.”

In September, AFT and UFT announced Microsoft had signed onto the AI safety and privacy agreement.

The AI Safety and Privacy Standard for Schools bars tech companies from using student and educator data to train AI models and from selling or using that data for advertising purposes. It also requires those companies to implement strong security protections and to design their tools to avoid harmful or manipulative experiences for students.

The unions’ agreement with Microsoft went into effect Nov. 1, and any school district nationwide that wants to add the AI safety and privacy standards to their new or current contracts with Microsoft can do so without being required to renew or renegotiate.

The Tuesday agreement with Anthropic formalizes that company’s own commitment to an agreement drafted by the unions in September.

AI can only “protect and enhance” teachers’ work “if teachers, students and school systems trust us,” Elizabeth Kelly, head of beneficial deployments at Anthropic, said in a Nov. 10 statement. “These agreements provide a foundation for that trust.”

Randi Weingarten, president of AFT, said in a statement that the agreement is "one step closer to an industry standard" now that Anthropic, a major player in the AI space, has joined.

“We said repeatedly that the guardrails for AI are just as important as any training we were doing for AI,” said Weingarten in the statement, adding that eventually the union hopes a standard will be "embedded in law."

“In the almost total absence of federal and state AI regulation, we want to make certain no teacher or parent ever has to choose between AI tools and the safety and privacy of their children," said Weingarten.

Michael Mulgrew, president of the United Federation of Teachers in New York City, said in a statement, "Ideally, the federal government would step in, but since it hasn’t, teachers unions are working to hold AI companies accountable."

The move comes as school systems nationwide have pushed back on the fast-growing technology.

In September, New York City — home to the nation's largest school system — announced that it was implementing the nation's “most expansive” AI moratorium for students.

The one-year pause prohibits student-facing AI tools for New York City Public Schools students in 2-K, a preschool program for 2-year-olds, through 8th grade during the 2026-27 school year. The temporary AI ban is expected to impact 600,000 students — or two-thirds of NYC’s public school enrollment.

The ban did not apply to teachers' use of AI.

That same month, Los Angeles Unified School District also announced it would restrict all students from using AI tools for the 2026-27 school year.

This Googlebook is driving me crazy

📅 Nov 10, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Right now, Googlebooks make more sense for Google than they do for users.

After trying for years to bring Android features to Chromebooks, Google decided to start over with Android as the foundation for a new laptop operating system. The first wave of Googlebooks are high-end laptops (priced $900 and up), with Google pitching them as the ultimate computers for Android enthusiasts.

But in their current form, Googlebooks are a disjointed mess, with websites and apps that don’t work quite right and AI features that aren’t fully fleshed out. While having a single operating system and app platform across laptops and mobile devices might make life easier for Google, it doesn’t yet translate to a better experience than the Chromebooks that Google aims to replace.

Android’s not ready for laptops

For the past month I’ve been using Acer’s Googlebook 14, which is the cheapest Googlebook at $900, and the only one whose touchscreen flips around into tablet mode. I have no major complaints about the hardware, which has a featherweight 2.51-pound chassis, a rich 120 Hz 3K OLED screen, and a smooth trackpad (albeit a “diving board” type whose click mechanism stiffens at the top edge).

My frustrations are more on the software side, where Android isn’t ready to carry a real laptop workload.

While Google is pushing developers to optimize their Android apps for large screens, keyboards, and trackpads, Google itself hasn’t always bothered to do so. The preloaded version of Gmail, for instance, is not an optimized Android app, but rather a web-based desktop app powered by the Chrome browser. Same goes for Google Docs, Drive, Meet, and YouTube. Tapping the menu button in these apps reveals a “Running in Chrome” disclaimer, and any Chrome extensions you install will apply to these apps as well.

This wouldn’t be a major concern if the web apps worked the way they’re supposed to. In Gmail, though, cursor hover controls don’t work, so you can’t quickly trash or archive messages line by line in the inbox. In Google Drive, documents open in a Chrome browser tab, while the same documents open in their own windows via Google Docs or Sheets. And if you try to select text in Google Docs using the touchscreen, the comment button pops up directly over the right text selector, making it unreachable.

Third-party Android apps can also have issues. Signing into Slack bounces me out to a Chrome tab, which then fails to authenticate back inside the Android app, so the only way to gain access is by manually entering a URL and password for each workplace. Even then, Slack’s Android app is poorly optimized, without the desktop version’s persistent sidebar.

Video apps still feel unfinished on Googlebooks as well. Those that Google deems “optimized for desktop,” such as Netflix and Disney+, will automatically open in full screen, which is jarring but at least fits the use case of watching video. Others, such as Fox One and NFL, open in a floating desktop window, and clicking their full screen icons accomplishes nothing. You’re actually supposed to ignore that button, highlight the maximize button in the window controls, then click the little “Full Screen” icon. Optimized or not, none of these apps support always-visible picture-in-picture mode like their mobile counterparts.

One last nitpick, admittedly a niche one: Bookmarklets don’t work on Googlebooks. I keep more than dozen of these in my browser’s address bar, which allows me to launch site-specific searches, create page excerpts, find archived versions of web pages, and remove “sticky” page elements. Not being able to use them on the Googlebook is a reminder that you’re not quite getting a full Chrome desktop experience.

The app situation will likely improve over time. When I started using the Googlebook, it wouldn’t let me install the Bluesky app and directed me to the web version. Now the app is available. Google Docs has also gained the ability to mark individual documents for offline use, which wasn’t possible at the outset. The Google Play Store has a tiered labeling system—“Optimized for Desktop,” “Compatible with Desktop,” “Better on the Website”—so you know what to expect, but for now the ecosystem is a work in progress.

Android synergies in progress

Googlebooks do have some neat features for Android users, the best of which is being able to access your phone’s files directly through the laptop’s Files app. There’s also “cross-device continuity,” which doesn’t work with many apps, but lets you quickly continue editing a message in Gmail or a document in Google Docs after opening it up on your phone.

App casting is rougher. If you have a phone running Android 17, this lets you view your phone’s apps through a Googlebook without installing them, and while this might be useful in some scenarios, it’s a subpar experience with jerky scrolling and occasional formatting issues. It can also lead to annoyances, like when a phone notification pops up on the Googlebook, and tapping it takes you into the janky app-casting version instead of the one that’s installed on your computer.

Android as a desktop operating system will also inherently pose some limitations. AI apps like ChatGPT and Claude lack the device control and folder-based file permissions that their desktop apps offer, and there are no command bar apps akin to Raycast for Windows and MacOS. The relative simplicity of an Android-based laptop may be a positive for some, but for me it’s a hindrance.

Too many Geminis

Beyond just catering to Android enthusiasts, Google is pitching Googlebooks as a premier surface for its Gemini AI assistant. In practice this means there are four main ways to invoke Gemini from the computer:

  • Wiggling your mouse cursor
  • Saying “Hey Google”
  • Clicking the Gemini icon in the dock
  • Clicking the Gemini icon in the Chrome taskbar

While having many entry points to Gemini makes sense, the execution feels disjointed. If you open the full Gemini app while a pop-up chat window is already open, for instance, the chat window closes and the full app cuts off your conversation, switching to a new one. The Chrome sidebar and pop-up window are also separate, so conversations in one don’t carry over to the other.

Those little inconsistencies tripped me up constantly, as I’d have to keep careful track of which conversation was happening where based on how I’d originally invoked it. Instead of just cramming AI touch points into different parts of the operating system, Google needs to do a better job of tying them all together.

There’s also a missed opportunity for Gemini to act more as an AI agent. While desktop AI apps on other platforms can work directly with files and folders on your computer, that’s currently not possible with Gemini on Googlebooks.

What’s next for Googlebooks?

Even if Googlebooks don’t feel ready now, they carry an air of inevitability. Google has already indicated that it will phase out Chrome OS by 2034, and it has outlined some vague plans for existing Chromebooks to turn into Googlebooks. Presumably that means Googlebooks will move down-market over time to include the kind of lower-end machines that defined the Chromebook business.

In the meantime, the question is whether Google will sufficiently invest in Googlebooks to address their weaknesses, instead of letting the project languish as it so often does (see: Stadia, Reader, its many attempts at social networking). One reason GoogleBooks feel so unpolished right now is because of Google’s hot-and-cold relationship with Android tablets, leading to a lack of app developer buy-in on devices with larger screens. With Google, there’s always a risk that it gets distracted by the next shiny object and leaves important work undone.

You can see how Googlebooks might eventually make sense: Combine a desktop-class Chrome experience with true Android app support, with easily available AI to help with research and automation. Maybe Google will get there someday, but first it needs to get more of the basics right.

‘The Odyssey’ Has Delivered Record Profits for IMAX

📅 Nov 10, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

‘The Odyssey’ Has Delivered Record Profits for IMAX

IMAX reported its strongest quarterly financial performance in the company’s history last week, with record box office, revenue, and profits for the third quarter of 2026.

Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey drove the results, becoming the highest-grossing IMAX release of all time.

THR reports that the company generated $712 million in global box office during the quarter, a 90% increase year over year and a significant rise from the $372 million recorded during the same period last year.

The Odyssey accounted for more than $550 million of that total in worldwide IMAX box office, contributing more than 30% of the film’s overall theatrical earnings. Its success was supported by premium screenings, including 70mm presentations that attracted audiences to IMAX locations.

Revenue increased 64% to $175 million, compared with $106.7 million in the third quarter of 2025. Net income climbed to $117 million, up from $22.6 million a year earlier.

“These results demonstrate the significant operating leverage and opportunity as we further expand the network and grow Imax box office,” says IMAX CFO Natasha Fernandes.

Content solutions revenue increased 110% to $94 million, reflecting the rise in global box office, while technology products and services revenue grew 28% to $77 million.

IMAX CEO Rich Gelfond says the results represented a broader shift in audience demand for theatrical experiences.

“What IMAX achieved goes beyond simply a ‘great quarter’ and transcends the many records we shattered in the period. What we believe we are witnessing is an awakening to the power and potential of our platform to impact global culture, unlock new commercial opportunities, and inspire a new level of demand and awe in audiences around the world,” he says, per THR.

“Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey is a historic cinematic achievement crafted entirely with IMAX technology and its record-breaking success marks a new era of opportunity for our company. The record margins we generated in the quarter demonstrate the unique strength of our model, and the growing value of scarce events and experiences in an increasingly AI-driven world underscore a powerful opportunity for our business, as we look ahead to a remarkably strong slate over the next several years.”

The company expects to significantly exceed its previous full-year 2026 box office guidance of $1.4 billion, which would itself represent a record. Its expansion programme is also continuing, with more than 100 agreements for IMAX systems signed worldwide so far this year. Approximately 65% of those agreements involve new locations.

THR notes that IMAX is also exploring new auditorium formats, including smaller premium venues designed to offer audiences an immersive viewing experience through larger aspect ratios, greater depth of view and improved sound. Additionally, the company is considering adding between 10 and 15 new 70mm film locations in response to demand and the upcoming film slate.

GTA 6 boss sends warning to pirates who make AI-generated PC version before official release

📅 Nov 10, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick has responded to the idea that unofficial, AI-assisted PC ports of Grand Theft Auto 6 could start popping up shortly after it is released.

Once November 19 hits, a 13-year-long wait for Grand Theft Auto fans will finally come to an end, as GTA 6 releases for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series S/X. However, the wait will go on – at least for an unannounced period – for PC players.

Rockstar Games have often taken up to a year before they release a PC version of their games, with GTA 5 and Red Dead Redemption 2 being two big examples of that. However, there have been suggestions that, with AI assistance, PC players could find themselves with unofficial ports of the game.

Former Rockstar Games dev Obbe Vermeij said it would cost “tens of thousands of dollars” to achieve, but didn’t rule it out.

“I don’t think it’s a financial matter, in terms of a threat to our business. I do think it’s a creative matter. It’s important to everyone, our developers and our consumers alike, to deliver the experience Rockstar envisions,” Zelnick told IGN. “And at the same time, of course, we protect our intellectual property vigilantly. So we are focused on these concerns.”

It isn’t the first time he has mentioned security concerns or enhancements either.  “We are utterly focused on enhancing our technical defenses and enhancing our legal activities appropriately. And at the same time, without in any way being cavalier, every entertainment business that exists is subject to some element of piracy,” Zelnick told investors at a Q&A.

“So this is likely to invade our business to a greater or lesser extent. I think it will be manageable and we are focused on it.”

GTA 6 boss defends delays with nod to Cyberpunk 2077’s launch

Former Rockstar dev says threat of unofficial AI ports could force GTA 6 onto PC sooner

Take-Two CEO gives positive update on eventual GTA 6 PC port

As noted, GTA 6’s PC release hasn’t yet been confirmed. There have been reports that it is slated to drop in the first quarter of 2027, which would be a rapid turnaround.

Additionally, there are questions surrounding the release of GTA Online in GTA 6, too. The multiplayer side of the game isn’t set to release alongside the single-player, but it should release “next year,” according to Twitch CEO Dan Clancy.

Clancy revealed that he had spent “a lot of time” talking to Rockstar about that, seeing as GTA RP is pretty big on Twitch.

Nvidia shares climbed about 2% in premarket trading on Tuesday to roughly $182.60, recovering part of Monday’s drop of more than 4% that left the stock near $179. The rebound comes as investors continue to weigh the fallout from CEO Jensen Huang’s admission that he had been unfaithful to his wife and had fallen short of his duties. Huang reportedly had a relationship with Alice Huang, an executive at Nvidia customer Megaspeed, whom US officials concluded was a Chinese intelligence asset. Nintendo Adds eShop Gifting to Switch Consoles

📅 Nov 10, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

The latest Nintendo Switch system update added support for an upcoming feature that will let users gift digital software purchased through the eShop. The gifting system is set to launch this month, meaning Switch users will be able to add digital games to their letters to Santa this festive season.

Nintendo continues to regularly release updates for the Switch and Switch 2, ensuring both consoles are in the best possible state and progressively improving user experience. Usually, these patch notes mostly focus on system stability, but that was not the case this time around. On Nov. 9, Nintendo released firmware update v23.5.0 for both Switch and Switch 2. Besides the usual technical updates, it added support for a highly requested feature: gifting.

Starting on Nov. 16, players will be able to purchase digital software (games, upgrade packs, or DLC) in the eShop and have it delivered to friends and family. This feature has been a long time coming, and Nintendo decided to add it at the right time — just in time for the holidays.

Once this feature is live, players will be able to tick the "Give as a Gift" box when buying a product on the eShop. Then, all they need to do is select the recipient, pick the wrapping color, and complete the purchase.

Digital gifts on the eShop will be sent immediately and cannot be scheduled, like on Steam. Unfortunately, this isn't the only setback. First, supervised accounts, meaning accounts under parental control, cannot use the gifting system. While details haven't been provided yet, there is a limit on how many gifts a user can send within a given time period. It is currently unknown whether the limit is based on the number of games, the type of software it is (DLC or game), or the value of the gift. Players cannot send gifts to users outside their family group, even if they are Switch friends.

These restrictions make sense, but some players were disappointed when they found out they couldn't gift all of their friends. Nintendo family groups have a maximum of eight members, which certainly makes this feature feel limited. Nevertheless, this addition is a step in the right direction.

Today’s consumers are spending more on things meaningful to their ‘life, health and happiness’, says Siam Piwat CEO Chadatip Chutrakul

📅 Nov 10, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Retailers across Asia are trying to find new ways to boost sales, whether it’s by giving shoppers more reasons to visit a retail location, or by using new technologies to reduce friction for customers, shortening the gap between attention and sales.

Consumers are spending more on things “that are meaningful to their life, health, and happiness,” Chadatip Chutrakul, CEO of Bangkok-based retail mall developer Siam Piwat, said at Fortune’s Southeast Asia 500 Summit in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam. “Retail is just a part of it… It’s not [only] about shopping, but creating experiential destinations.”

In October, Siam Piwat announced ICONPHUKET, a retail and entertainment development in Thailand’s Phuket province. Scheduled to open in 2029, the project will include green spaces and health and wellness facilities alongside shops, residences, offices and hotels.

“Shopping malls in Thailand—and I think in Asia—are like a second home to customers,” Chutrakul explained. “So besides shopping, we [also try to] offer everything else.”

Malina Ngai, CEO of global drug and beauty chain AS Watson, agreed that today’s consumers need a reason to choose one particular retailer over another. “Ultimately, the retail game is about relevance,” she said. “It’s not so much about whether you have more products or technology… customers are looking for a brand that they trust.”

Online, social media and influencers are pushing consumers to develop relationships with brands faster.

“[In the past], consumers built a relationship with a brand over [a span of] five years, but that cycle has been cut down to a couple of months now, because people start to adhere to a brand identity very quickly,” Saemin Ahn, managing partner at Rakuten Capital, the venture capital arm of Japanese conglomerate Rakuten Group, said.

Platforms also need to ensure views are turned into purchases. In February, Rakuten Ichiba—the company’s online marketplace—partnered with Google via the YouTube Shopping affiliate program, which allows viewers to tap ‘View Products’ during YouTube videos and navigate straight to Rakuten Ichiba’s webpage to make a purchase.

“In Rakuten Ichiba, there’s about 40,000 to 50,000 merchants that we have to keep happy, and those happy merchants keep the users happy,” Ahn explained.

Physical retailers are also using new tools to help shoppers find what they need. AS Watson is using AI to study how customers shop in different sections of its stores, from supplements to oral and hair care, Ngai said. The aim is to identify where shoppers struggle and change the layout or signage to help them.

“If we know that they spend about 56 seconds on this aisle, and they couldn’t find the product they need, we would have to improve how we arrange our products, put up signages, and work with our suppliers to make it easier for customers to make decisions,” she said.

Angelica Ang is a Singapore-based journalist who covers the Asia-Pacific region.

Q: “My Spouse Complains About My ADHD Constantly!”

📅 Nov 10, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

“Start with an honest conversation that acknowledges the effects of your ADHD on your partner and explains how it thwarts your efforts to be the best possible spouse .”

Q: “How can I help my husband understand my ADHD so he’s not just complaining all the time about how hard this is for him?”

First, begin by acknowledging the truth of what he is saying: Your ADHD does, indeed, have tangible effects on him. It also has emotional effects; he likely burns much more mental energy than you can see worrying about whether you completed agreed-upon tasks.

Let down your guard for an honest conversation about the impact of your actions (or inaction) on him. Show him that he matters to you and that you empathize with his experience. You may need to spend significant time here; don’t move on until you’re positive that he really feels that you get it.

[Get This Free Download: Manage ADHD’s Impact on Your Relationship]

This sets the stage for the second part of the conversation — how ADHD thwarts your efforts to be the best possible partner. In other words, you have good intentions, even if they aren’t obvious, and you can feel equally frustrated and disappointed by what makes him upset. Also, your ADHD makes your life harder, not just his. While his complaints might be accurate, his too-frequent criticisms are not helping.

Finally, discuss how you can work together to address your hotspots. Ask: What can each of us do, or at least try to do, differently to smooth out some of our pain points? For example, do you want reminders? If so, how and when? Also, does he want to give those reminders?

It’s also helpful to discuss protocols when things don’t go according to plan. How and when can he bring up his concerns in a way that you can hear without getting defensive? How can you tell him that his proposed solution is not working for you?

Encourage your partner to focus on their experience rather than dissecting your actions and making declarations about why you did something.

For example, it’s more effective to say, “It stresses me out when you don’t follow through on commitments because then I feel like I have to take over, and I really don’t want to keep doing that,” versus saying, “You don’t worry about doing things because you know I’ll just do it if you don’t.”

[Download: 5 Ways to Improve Emotional Control at Home]

I often recommend focusing your conversations on what you want in the future, not what happened in the past.

Toxic secrets are hiding in Arctic ice

📅 Nov 10, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

A century-old pollution trail leads scientists back to Montana mining

At the turn of the twentieth century, the Anaconda Smelter in Montana spewed arsenic into the air — those heavy metal particles that are now trapped in Arctic ice cores.

Ice cores record Earth’s secrets, even the dirty ones.

Some of the cylindrical sections of ice extracted from the Arctic contain elevated levels of arsenic, lead and other heavy metals that circulated in our planet’s atmosphere in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Those pollutants, which have been tied to declines in IQ and higher rates of certain cancers, were probably emitted by a mining and smelting company in Montana whose grounds are now designated as multiple Superfund sites, the researchers report November 3 in Nature Sustainability.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The ice cores contain tiny particles that were once airborne — including pollutants, volcanic ash and salt from ocean spray — and fell to our planet’s surface within a few days or weeks. In polar regions, that fallout combines with snow and is preserved as ice.

Joseph McConnell, an environmental scientist at the Desert Research Institute, and his collaborators recently analyzed 10 ice cores collected across Canada, Greenland and Russia. The cores contained material that had fallen to Earth as early as 210 BCE, but the interval spanning the Industrial Revolution in the United States — from roughly 1870 to 1914 — was what caught the team’s collective eye.

In the ice layers from that period, arsenic concentrations in some of the ice cores were up to 15 times higher than pre-Industrial Revolution levels. Because the heavy metal exposure has been tied to upticks in the rates of certain cancers, McConnell and his team set out to determine the most likely source of all that pollution.

The largest increases in arsenic existed in the ice cores from Greenland. That finding was a big hint, McConnell says, because atmospheric circulation patterns tend to move material from west to east. “The only way you can explain that pattern of deposition is if the emissions are coming from North America,” McConnell says. “Had it been from Europe, we would have seen much larger increases in the Russian Arctic.”

The most likely source, the team concluded, was a massive copper mining and smelting operation in southwestern Montana operated by the Anaconda Copper Mining Company. It was one of the largest in North America during the Industrial Revolution and, unlike other copper mining operations in the area, it worked with copper ore that contained heavy metals like arsenic and lead. It was no secret that those toxic metals were entering the atmosphere, says Fred Quivik, a historian and the author of Smoke and Tailings, a book about the environmental history of copper smelting in Montana. “Ranchers and farmers started seeing their livestock die from arsenic poisoning.”

Based on the concentrations of arsenic in the ice cores and models of how material disperses in the atmosphere, McConnell and his colleagues estimated that the Anaconda Copper Mining Company was emitting roughly 30 tons of arsenic per day into the atmosphere in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. By comparison, Chile, currently the world’s largest producer of copper and home to more than 20 mining operations, collectively emits roughly one quarter as much arsenic today.

Beginning in 1919, the Anaconda Copper Mining Company installed devices near its smokestacks and other facilities to capture arsenic and prevent its release into the atmosphere. Arsenic emissions dropped by about 60 percent as a result, the ice core data showed, but by then hundreds of thousands of nearby residents had already been exposed for decades. That exposure could have been lessened, McConnell says, if the Anaconda Copper Mining Company hadn’t waited so long to install the pollution-abatement technology. “They delayed installation for about a decade.”

These new findings should be combined with census records to trace the effects of this pollution on human health in the 19th and 20th centuries, McConnell and his team suggest. “We hope that epidemiologists will take this information and really investigate potential impacts on human populations.”

Announcing Long-Context Training on TPUs with MaxText Context Parallelism

📅 Nov 10, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Long-context training — including pretraining and post-training, has become a foundation of frontier AI models. Longer native sequence lengths give large language models (LLMs) the working memory to read a whole code repository or ingest hours of video, and reason through multi-step agentic tasks. In three years, context windows have grown from 128K–200K tokens to 1M–2M, and models trained toward 10M tokens are arriving. Training at those lengths, not just serving them, is where the system limits show up.

In particular, efficient training at multi-million-token sequence lengths runs into the following bottlenecks:

Today, we are excited to announce long-context training support in MaxText, Google Cloud's open-source JAX training framework. MaxText enables this by supporting four context-parallel strategies on Cloud TPU: All-gather, A2A (DeepSpeed Ulysses), P2P (Ring Attention), and the A2A + P2P hybrid (Unified Sequence Parallelism, or USP), combined with load balancing and sequence packing. All four use the Tokamax Splash Attention kernel. Combined with the 3D inter-chip interconnect (ICI) ( supported on TPUs such as TPU 5p or TPU 7 (Ironwood) ), this lets one sequence span an entire slice while communication overlaps compute and memory per chip stays flat. In our benchmarks, Llama 3.1 8B (25 head dim, 16 query heads) demonstrates exceptional long-context efficiency, achieving 70% Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) on TPU 5p for sequence lengths up to 4 million tokens. Across both TPU 5p and TPU 7, context can be seamlessly extended to 14 million tokens—with TPU 7 consistently maintaining 50% MFU across all sequence scales below 6 million tokens.

This functionality is available today in MaxText v0.2.4(doc).

Context parallelism splits a long sequence across chips, so no chip holds the activations of the whole sequence. Context parallelism can be combined with data and tensor parallelism, and the smallest context-parallel size that fits your sequence in HBM is usually the right one. This also holds for sparser attention variants which cut attention compute but not the activations of every other layer.

Attention is the one global operation where every token needs the keys and values of every preceding token, so each context parallel strategy has to bring those keys and values back together. Each makes a different tradeoff between memory (how much KV a chip holds), communication (how much moves per layer, and whether it overlaps compute), and model shape (how many attention heads to split).

All-gather: Each chip keeps its chunk of the sequence and, at every layer, gathers the keys and values from every other chip. It is the simplest option. However, because causal masking causes later tokens to attend to larger prefixes, All-gather requires balancing compute load across devices.

Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video

All-to-All (Ulysses): Gathering keys and values makes every chip hold the whole sequence, so attention memory never shrinks no matter how many chips you add. All-to-All changes what each chip owns instead. Attention is independent across heads but not across tokens, so the head axis is free to shard and the token axis is not. An All-to-All before attention rotates the sharding from one onto the other: each chip gives up the heads it is not responsible for and receives the tokens it was missing for the heads it keeps, ending up with the full sequence for a few heads instead of a few tokens for all heads. This is also why Ulysses does not need token load balancing. Attention then runs as ordinary single-chip attention with standard kernels, and a second All-to-All rotates the output back. KV per chip shrinks by the context-parallel factor, but you cannot split across more chips than the model has heads — and tensor parallelism shards that same dimension, so TP × CP is capped by the head count (under GQA, by the KV heads: eight for Llama 3 8B). The all-to-all itself, though, does not overlap with compute — attention cannot start on a partial sequence, so every chip waits for data from every other chip before any of them begins.

Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video

P2P (ring attention): Ulysses' ceiling is the head count; ring attention removes it by never leaving the token axis. Keys and values never materialize in full. KV chunks travel around a ring of chips one hop at a time, neighbor to neighbor. Each chip attends its queries to the chunk it holds while the next one is in flight, and merges the partial results as it goes. A chip holds its own chunk and one visiting chunk, never the full sequence, and the communication overlaps compute. However, dividing attention computation into smaller chunks can reduce local kernel efficiency, and unlike All-to-All Ulysses, ring attention requires explicit load balancing.

Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video

A2A + P2P (USP): A2A + P2P (USP): Neither strategy scales on its own — All-to-All stops at the head count, and a long ring accumulates hops while thinning the overlap that makes it work. Unified sequence parallelism composes them on two axes of the chip mesh, so the context-parallel degree becomes the product of the two: All-to-All along one axis, sized at or below the KV-head count, and a ring along the other to extend past it. Because each All-to-All group has already pooled its tokens, a ring step now carries a chunk larger by the All-to-All factor, and the ring is correspondingly shorter — more compute per hop to hide the transfer behind, and fewer hops to accumulate latency and causal imbalance. On Cloud TPU the two map onto two axes of the slice's chip mesh.

Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video

These strategies cover the attention variants in today's major models, from multi-head and grouped-query attention to DeepSeek-style multi-head latent attention.

Splitting the sequence only pays off if the attention compute on each chip stays efficient. All four strategies run on Splash Attention, the block-sparse flash attention kernel from Tokamax, Google's open-source library of TPU kernels. It skips fully masked blocks and handles packed sequences without padding. P2P calls it once per ring step, on the local queries and the KV chunk that has just arrived, while the transfer for the next step runs underneath, in the forward and backward pass alike. Each chip does the same fused, block-level work it would do without context parallelism, with the communication hidden behind it.

P2P (Ring Attention) is the primary workhorse for very long-context training, whereas All-Gather is the standard baseline for most other cases where the KV can fit. These are the primary CP strategies to use in practice. We compare how far each can push context length on a fixed 64-chip TPU 5p slice with Llama 3.1 8B (256 head dim, 16 query heads) , and measure their MFUs. In ideal settings where both strategies can have large enough chunks (S/CP) and local batch size - the two major variables driving MFU on TPU 5p, we observe that P2P can outperform All-Gather almost every context length from 64K to 14M tokens, where communication becomes mostly hidden with the Ring circular transport schedule.

TPU v7x (Ironwood) takes the same recipe further. With twice the HBM per chip, P2P training of 14M tokens on 64 TPU 7 chips reached 48.7% Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) compared to 37.1% on TPU 5p. We observed that ring attention performs better than other context parallelism strategies -- e.g. Ulysses and USP –- on TPU 7 chips.

The choice of context parallelism strategy depends mostly on whether the gathered KV fits in HBM, and on how many KV heads the model has:

For all CP strategies, when you run low on memory: Offload before you recompute. MaxText can move saved activations, optimizer states, and parameters to host memory tensor by tensor. At long context lengths, these transfers are hidden behind compute, making offloading effectively free. Offload attention outputs first, followed by optimizer states, layer inputs, parameters, and finally remat as a last resort. MFU stays flat through the offload steps while all-gather falls off and eventually stops fitting. For more details, see the remat tuning guide.

Looking ahead, we see two natural extensions. The first is broader model coverage. Models that mix sliding-window and global layers, such as Gemma, would run the window layers with a short exchange between neighboring chips while the global layers use the ring. We also plan to support linear attention mechanisms such as Gated Delta Net (GDN) and Kimi Delta Attention (KDA). The second is performance, with further tuning of the Tokamax kernels and the P2P backward pass to narrow the remaining gap to all-gather at short context, and recipes by model and context length for TPU 5p and 7 chips.

Context parallelism is available today in MaxText v0.2.4 on PyPI, the corresponding Docker images and on GitHub main. Sample recipes are available here for TPU 7 and TPU 5p. Pick a strategy with context_parallel_strategy (ring, ulysses, or usp), set the context-parallel size, and keep the rest of your run the same. The sharding guide has the flags and constraints for each strategy, and the release notes link to the pull requests behind this work. We can't wait to see what you train.

What is Pathways? Single-controller training for large models

What is Pathways? Single-controller training for large models

📅 Nov 10, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video

Today, we announce the General Availability of Pathways on Google Cloud Platform. In this post, you will learn about Pathways, the distributed system Google built to train its own large models, including Gemini. We discuss how Pathways addresses the coordination challenge by introducing one client that describes the whole computation as a graph, and how the distributed runtime places it, moves the tensors, and keeps the accelerators busy.

Most large-model training runs as Single Program, Multiple Data (SPMD) programs. Every accelerator runs the same program in lockstep and coordinates through collectives like AllReduce.

It works well when your job is the same program running on every device. It struggles when the job is no longer uniform, like a pipeline whose stages wait on each other or an RL loop where a sampler, a reward model, and a trainer are different programs that have to overlap.

Large runs also have to survive hardware failures, which interrupted Gemini 2.5 training multiple times per hour. In SPMD, one lost machine stops every process and sends the run back to its last checkpoint. In each case, the challenge is coordination. You have to decide what runs where and in what order, how tensors move between devices, and how the job keeps going when a machine drops out.

In this post of the series “Pathways on Google Cloud”, you will learn about Pathways, the distributed system Google built to train its own large models, including Gemini. The post discusses how Pathways addresses the coordination challenge by introducing one client that describes the whole computation as a graph, and how the distributed runtime places it, moves the tensors, and keeps the accelerators busy.

By the end, you'll know where SPMD is suboptimal, what single-controller execution changes, and how Pathways coordinates a whole training job across a cluster.

If you train PyTorch models, you almost certainly use Distributed Data Parallel (DDP) or Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP). DDP runs a copy of your script on every accelerator and averages gradients with a collective operation such as AllReduce. FSDP shards parameters, gradients, and optimizer states across workers so that the model fits at all.

Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video

DDP and FSDP both follow the Single Program, Multiple Data (SPMD) execution model. Every process runs the same copy of your script, owns its accelerators for the whole run, and moves in lockstep with the others, because the only way they coordinate is through collectives like AllReduce. Inside one tightly connected group of accelerators those collectives run over a fast interconnect and are cheap. Scale the job across groups and the same collectives cross the datacenter network, which is far slower. On a TPU v5p, for example, each chip gets 1,200 GB/s of bidirectional chip-to-chip bandwidth inside its group, but only 50 Gb/s (gigabits, about 6 GB/s) to the datacenter network which is roughly two orders of magnitude less.

And because every step blocks on its collectives, that communication lands directly in step time. The more groups you span, the larger the share of each step spent moving data, so throughput grows slower than the number of accelerators you add.

As long as your training job is one program that fills the hardware you give it, this execution model fits well. You write your model as if there were one device, and the collectives do the rest. But fitting a model into memory is only part of the problem. Keeping every accelerator busy is the harder part, and this is where the SPMD model starts to show its limits.

Take pipeline parallelism as an example. You split a model into blocks across devices, and each device now runs different code over smaller micro-batches. Activations flow forward, activation gradients flow back, and while device 0 works on the first micro-batch, devices 1 and 2 wait. Apart from the idle accelerators you keep paying for, this drops utilization and throughput, even though every device has work in the steady state.

Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video

Another example is RL post-training for an LLM. You have a sampler that generates rollouts, a reward model that scores them, and a trainer that updates the policy and sends the new weights back to the sampler. These are three different programs that should overlap; otherwise the sampler is idle while the trainer runs, and the trainer is idle while the sampler generates.

Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video

In both scenarios, the job is now several different programs running on different devices, and their dependencies can no longer be managed through a single collective. You now have to coordinate which devices share which tensors, which processes run while others are still finishing, and how early to enqueue the next buffer so an accelerator never waits for input. Because each worker only has visibility into its local devices and data, no individual process can manage all of these dependencies itself. That has several consequences.

First, because each process owns its accelerators for the whole run and every collective blocks until all devices finish, one failed machine prevents the collective from completing and stops the entire job, forcing a restart from the last checkpoint. You cannot add devices mid-run, and you cannot give devices back.

Second, because each process holds its accelerators from start to finish, capacity can't move to where it's needed. Within one job, a stage that needs fewer chips than another still keeps the extra ones. They sit idle, you keep paying for them, and no other part of the job can use them until the run ends. Across a team, the same happens at cluster scale. Every job owns its accelerators for as long as it runs, so sharing a cluster means splitting it into per-job allocations, and each new job brings up its own processes on its own hosts.

Finally, the development process itself gets harder. On one host you iterate fast because you run the script, drop into a Python shell, set a breakpoint, and debug. This is not true once the job spans many hosts. You need a launcher to push your script to every host, you hit coordination bugs that never showed up on one machine, and there's no single process to break into. When something hangs, each worker is stuck at a collective waiting for the others, with no one place that shows the whole job.

So the common challenge here is the coordination itself. As soon as the job stops being one program in lockstep, you have to decide what runs where, in what order, and how tensors get from one device to the next.

One way to describe this is as a graph, where each block is a node, each tensor that moves between blocks is an edge, and the devices are where the nodes are placed. You can wire that graph up by hand in SPMD, one process at a time. But what if a single client declared that graph, including what each block does, what it needs, and where it runs, and a distributed runtime handled the transfers, dependencies, and ordering along its edges?

Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video

That is the idea behind Pathways, the distributed system Google built to train its own largest models, including Gemini. Pathways runs JAX programs on TPUs and it is available on Google Cloud.

With Pathways, you define the end-to-end computation from a single Python client, without writing custom coordination code, and a distributed runtime executes it. That client is decoupled from the hardware. It runs on an ordinary CPU machine and you write your program against virtual devices; a resource manager maps them onto real chips, and a worker on each accelerator host runs the compiled programs it receives.

Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video

Because your code refers to virtual devices rather than physical ones, the runtime is flexible to allow users to change the devices used for a given computation. This allows you to stay in control while the runtime handles the mapping to hardware. In an RL loop, for example, the trainer and the samplers rarely want the same number of chips, so you can give the sampler stage more chips by asking for more virtual devices.

Also, the same capability helps when a host fails or the hardware isn't ready yet. If a host dies, the resource manager remaps the work onto healthy chips and the run keeps going instead of relaunching the whole job, which is the basis for elastic training. And because the program targets virtual devices, compilation can start before the physical chips are provisioned, so setup overlaps with provisioning instead of waiting on it.

The resource manager owning the chips also means one Pathways cluster can serve several clients, so researchers on a team can share its capacity. With the Shared Pathways Service, the cluster stays up as a long running service, which lets you develop interactively on TPUs hosted on GKE. Each client connects on demand from a laptop or VM, gets its own slices (groups of tightly connected TPU chips) from the shared pool, and hands them back when it disconnects. When every chip is busy, the next workload waits until capacity frees up.

Take the three-block model from Figure 2. Block A runs on one group of devices, block B on a second, block C on a third. You declare what each block computes, its target devices, and where its outputs go. Pathways expresses those dependencies as a distributed dataflow graph, in which each block is a compiled SPMD program and each edge is a tensor the runtime has to deliver.

Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video

In a single SPMD program, the framework handles the collectives that keep the devices in sync within a group, with or without Pathways, and your code doesn't change. The difference shows up once the job runs several programs on different groups (Multiple Programs, Multiple Data, MPMD), like these three blocks or the sampler, reward model, and trainer of an RL loop. Then no single process sees both sides (the same limit from before, where each worker only knows its own devices), so getting a tensor from block A to block B is a hand-off you have to coordinate yourself.

Pathways closes that gap. You declare the dependency once, and the runtime moves and reshards the tensor for you, over the fast interconnect within a group and over the datacenter network between groups.

To keep the accelerators busy, Pathways prepares launches ahead of time with futures and parallel asynchronous dispatch. While block A is still computing, block B can't run yet, but its input shapes and dtypes are already known, so the runtime allocates B's buffers and schedules the transfer before A's output even exists. Host-side setup for every block happens up front, and each block launches when its inputs arrive.

Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video

This is also what keeps the single client from becoming a bottleneck. Because dispatch is asynchronous, the coordination work overlaps with the compute already running on the chips, so the client stays off the critical path instead of stalling the accelerators between steps.

In Pathways, the runtime decides execution order when a group has more than one operation ready. In pipelined training, B's devices often hold both the forward pass for an upcoming micro-batch and the backward pass for an earlier one. If each device picked on its own, their collectives would conflict and the group would stall.

Pathways has a central scheduler that puts every program's operations into one consistent order, so operations that must communicate start together instead of deadlocking.

Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video

And because it's still one client, the development loop we mentioned before comes back. It's the same single Python process whether you drive one host or thousands of hosts, so you can drop into a shell, set a breakpoint, and inspect the run as it goes. When something stalls, there's one place that knows what's queued on every device and which dependency hasn't been met, instead of a hang spread across separate processes.

Put together, Pathways separates model building from execution. You choose how the model partitions across hardware using the client. And the runtime handles the transfers, ordering, and scheduling that keep accelerators busy, across the whole cluster rather than just your slice of it.

Described this way, Pathways can start to sound like an orchestrator you already know. If scheduling work, moving tensors, and keeping a whole cluster busy brings Ray to mind, it should. But the two work at different layers.

Ray is an open-source framework for orchestrating Python-native AI workloads across large clusters. It provisions the cluster, schedules your Python code as tasks and actors, and launches your workload across hosts, holding data loading, training, serving, and tuning under one control plane. To Ray, an accelerator is a resource to schedule.

What Ray doesn't change is how your training runs on the chips. The job inside each worker still runs as SPMD. The framework inserts the collectives, and each process sees only its own devices. Ray places and starts that job but it doesn't turn it into a single program that drives the whole cluster.

That is the layer Pathways works at. It changes the execution model underneath, so one client coordinates every chip. Because they sit at different layers, the two are complementary. In principle, Ray can orchestrate the cluster and the pipeline while Pathways handles how the training step executes.

So concretely, Ray's job is about orchestration while Pathways' job is about execution. With Ray, you tie your data, training, serving, and tuning together and spread heterogeneous work across accelerators and clouds. With Pathways, you run one model across many groups of chips, express patterns beyond SPMD, and recover from a failed host instead of relaunching the whole job.

When a training job stops being one uniform program, the challenge becomes coordinating the dependencies between stages, the tensors that cross the network, and the ordering that keeps every accelerator fed.

SPMD requires you to address these dependencies. With Pathways, you describe the computation once, from a single client, as a graph of blocks and the tensors between them. And you have a runtime that places the blocks on virtual devices, moves and reshards the tensors, orders the work across the cluster, and remaps around a failed host.

With Pathways, model building and execution are separated and you reason about the whole cluster instead of one slice of it.

Amy Poehler And Steve Carell Bonded Over How Poorly The Office And Parks And Rec Went Their First Seasons

📅 Nov 10, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →
